chunks: I am Abu al-Hasan, the one who killed your grandfather, your uncle, and your brother by cutting them to pieces on the day of Badr. That sword is with me, and with that heart I meet my enemy. I have not changed the religion, nor introduced a new prophet, and indeed I am upon the path which you left willingly and entered into reluctantly.
ai.seo_question: Who did Ali kill at Badr according to his letter to Muawiya?
ai.summary: Sharif al-Radi includes this passage in his correspondence to Muawiya to establish Ali’s legitimacy as the rightful successor by contrasting his voluntary, pure adherence to the Prophet’s legacy with Muawiya’s coerced entry into Islam. The mention of the specific sword serves as a tangible symbol of his martial prowess and divine favor, while the assertion of 'not changing the religion' directly counters Umayyad claims of innovation or deviation. This letter underscores the core Shia narrative of continuity (ittiba') versus the political expediency of the Umayyads.
